item.title: Mind-wandering preserves word-level coupling while disrupting comprehension
item.description: arXiv:2611.14814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Readers can move their eyes through a page but retain little of its meaning when their minds wander. We tested whether word properties still guide their eyes during these lapses. We analyzed public eye-tracking and electroencephalography (EEG) data from 44 adults who read articles. They marked the text read during each lapse they noticed. We linked these spans to the sentences needed for later comprehension questions. Word frequency, length and surprisal still predicted which words readers skipped and how long they looked at them. Compared with on-task reading, these effects met equivalence bounds of $\pm$10% for skipping and $\pm$20% for gaze duration. Readers spent 14.6% longer on words during lapses. Yet readers answered less accurately when lapses covered sentences needed for a later question. The adjusted difference was 25.7 percentage points for lapses covering all versus none of these sentences. The fixation-related EEG response was 42.7% smaller during lapses. At left posterior-lateral sensor P7, the median increase in alpha power was 10.0%. Occipital sensor Oz showed no reliable increase. These results suggest that word properties can guide the eyes while readers fail to form or retain a useful representation of the text.
item.dc:creator: Anirudh Natarajan, Paul Sajda

item.title: Same currents, different field: $\Delta f = 0$ carrier-only stimulation is not temporal interference without the beat
item.description: arXiv:2611.14839v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Carrier-only stimulation ($\Delta f = 0$) is generally considered the most rigorous control for temporal interference (TI) stimulation, assumed to reproduce TI's kilohertz carrier field without its low-frequency beat. We show that this assumption is incorrect: without the frequency difference, the carrier fields interfere coherently, changing the peak strength, power, and direction of the resulting field depending on electrode polarity and montage geometry. Using computational field modeling, we demonstrate that these mismatches can be substantial and widespread. We therefore recommend that TI studies report electrode polarity, model both carrier-field exposures, and choose controls according to their study objectives.
item.dc:creator: Ido Haber, Giulio Tononi, Larissa Albantakis

item.title: Prototypes of the Mind: A Unified Framework for Probing the Visual Brain
item.description: arXiv:2611.15046v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep learning has driven substantial progress in modeling fMRI responses, yet most existing approaches are optimized for a single objective---such as neural encoding, stimulus decoding, or post hoc interpretation---making it difficult to obtain a coherent account of neural representations. We introduce a unified framework that connects vision foundation models to brain activity while supporting neural analysis from multiple complementary perspectives. Our approach replaces black-box features with a sparse, interpretable representation composed of visual prototypes, and links these prototypes to voxel responses through a linear readout. This design makes the model transparent at both levels: prototype activations expose the visual concepts present in the stimulus, while the learned linear weights characterize each voxel's selectivity. Using this interface, we identify which visual concepts drive neural responses and where they appear in the image, reveal cortical organization through voxel tuning in prototype space, and perform controlled stimulus synthesis to probe cortical selectivity through targeted interventions. Together, these results establish prototype-based representations as a unified and interpretable foundation for studying visual representations in the human brain.
item.dc:creator: Shi Chen, Seoyoung Ahn, Doris Tsao

item.title: Analysis choices decide whether untrained networks beat trained ones at V1: a multiverse analysis of model-brain RSA
item.description: arXiv:2611.15533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Untrained convolutional networks have been reported to rival trained networks as models of visual cortex, and we had reported an untrained-network advantage over backpropagation at V1 in THINGS fMRI, together with a dependence on evaluation resolution. Under a pre-specified ridge readout, the untrained network scored below the trained one at every pooling grid (median r difference -0.043 at g = 4, 0 of 5 seeds positive), and also in MSE skill and per-fold r. In exploratory analyses, across 36 combinations of unit normalisation, distance measure and voxel normalisation (28 distinct analyses), the sign of the V1 contrast depended on the analysis (intervals above 0 in 5 and below 0 in 9 distinct analyses), and in our networks the resolution dependence of the original convention appeared in only one cell. Raw correlation-distance representational similarity analysis (RSA) covaried with the alignment of model and voxel patterns with the unit-mean profile (Spearman 0.97 across our networks, 0.79 across six ImageNet architectures); the advantage was absent from the component orthogonal to the mean profile, and the parallel component alone did not resolve it. On the unweighted angular component of centred patterns, trained networks were ahead at V1 (our network and 5 of 6 ImageNet models) and at LOC (all seven); the norm-weighted angular term was not resolved. A luminance-and-contrast bank scored above every network under ridge (point estimates), and adding network features under a shared penalty did not improve prediction. Intervals are stimulus-bootstrap intervals for three subjects, and 6 pre-stated predictions were not met. We recommend reporting sensitivity to centring over the evaluated stimuli on both sides, reporting components separately, and including a small multiverse and simple baselines.
item.dc:creator: Nils Leutenegger

item.title: Optogenetic Modulation Fraction: A Robust Opsin-Presence Effect and an Unresolved Cell-Type Question, by Censoring-Aware Survival Analysis of Public Neuropixels Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.15606v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Expressing channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) in an interneuron population substantially raises the fraction of locally recorded units whose spike timing is altered by light, relative to no-opsin controls, under every method tried. Establishing that result rigorously, and retracting two secondary claims that did not survive the same rigor, is this paper's actual content. We reanalyze eight public Allen Institute Neuropixels sessions (4,112 units), modeling light-to-first-spike latency as a right-censored time-to-event outcome, with a Cox model, pooled FDR correction, and a small-cluster-robust test (logistic regression plus an exact wild cluster bootstrap, since only eight session clusters exist). We report an unrestricted modulation fraction and a restricted direct-responder fraction (evoked latency under 10 ms, an explicit, literature-grounded threshold). ChR2-expressing Sst/Pvalb sessions show a large, bootstrap-confirmed elevation over control under both metrics. Two further claims, each initially suggested by a standard test, did not survive the exact bootstrap or a direct formal check, and we report both retractions as results in their own right. Vip-ChR2's apparent elevation over control is not confirmed by the bootstrap and becomes non-significant once restricted to direct responders. A second pattern, that among modulated units Vip sessions had a higher proportion of direct responses than Sst/Pvalb, opposite the raw ordering, evaporated under the same bootstrap test: no genotype contrast approaches significance, and control has the highest proportion of all three, which cannot be biological. Per-session rates vary enormously within one genotype. With two earlier corrections (a session-composition artifact and a standard-versus-exact-bootstrap discrepancy), this is a four-correction paper: pooled estimates and secondary patterns deserve the same scrutiny as a headline claim.
item.dc:creator: Siddhardha Nanda

item.title: Pyramidal Columns Acting as Attention Heads
item.description: arXiv:2611.16057v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? More specifically, could a suitable group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language regions (PTLRs) constitute the biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head, under a mathematical instantiation that need not coincide with its standard Transformer instantiation? This paper investigates this hypothesis by examining possible correspondences between the functional organization of attention heads and neurophysiological mechanisms operating within and across pyramidal columns involved in human language processing. Our analysis builds on a mechanical-structural description of Transformer attention heads as systems of simple neural networks linked through output-input and output-weight interconnections. We examine the functional organization of an attention head and the input-dependent transformations it produces, and ask how the corresponding processing relations could be constructed in biological neural tissue. We then identify candidate neural mechanisms of signal transmission and modulation within and across pyramidal columns that may jointly support such a construction. On this basis, we propose that a suitably organized group of pyramidal columns in PTLRs could constitute a biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head. Whether the required functional organization actually exists in PTLRs remains an open empirical question. The hypothesis does not require the biological system to reproduce the standard mathematical instantiation of Transformer attention: the same functional architecture may be mechanically realized and mathematically instantiated in a different way, consistent with its biological construction.
item.dc:creator: Fabrizia Giulia Garavaglia, Marco Giunti

item.title: Dynamical mean-field theory of latching Potts networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.16999v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spontaneous transitions between memories, as observed in internally generated cognition such as mind-wandering and free association, require neural dynamics capable of destabilizing one attractive memory state and moving towards another. We ask what minimal representational structure is required for such transitions to emerge in random associative networks. To address this question, we study Potts associative networks with $S$ active states per unit and slow adaptive thresholds. The $S=1$ case can model a standard Hopfield-like network of binary units. We employ dynamical mean-field theory in the extensive-load regime, where the number of stored patterns scales linearly with network size and connectivity, and we focus on transitions between two condensed memories, which are singled out in the connectivity matrix. In the finite-load regime, we show that transitions are governed by an effective drive term, whose sign and temporal evolution distinguish high-latching (structured), low-latching (random), and non-latching regimes. The resulting phase diagram shows that adaptation alone is not sufficient: transitions only occur within certain ranges of the overlap between the two memories. In the binary case $S=1$, in particular, no unit can be active in both memories but in different Potts states, thus strongly supressing the high-latching, structured transitions that exist for $S>1$. In the extensive-load regime, non-condensed memories generate colored fluctuations and retarded self-interactions through an effective memory kernel. We find that latching trajectories change the effective timescale of this kernel, a dynamical signature of transitions in the extensive-load regime. These results indicate that multi-state Potts-like representations are essential for structured memory-to-memory transitions, a hallmark of spontaneous thought.
item.dc:creator: Anindita Basu, Carlo Orientale Caputo, Fernando Lucas Metz, Alessandro Treves

item.title: Random Exploration is Random
item.description: arXiv:2611.17011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decision making often requires balancing exploitation of familiar options with exploration of uncertain alternatives. One strategy for exploration is random exploration, in which choices become more variable and less tied to the option that currently appears best. However, it remains unclear whether this variability reflects genuine stochasticity or instead a deterministic structure that traditional cognitive models fail to capture. We examined this question using the Horizon Task in an aggregated dataset of 1,392 participants completing over 1,270,695 trials. In this task, exploration becomes more valuable when participants have more future choices, and choice variability increases under longer horizons. We tested whether more expressive neural network models could recover deterministic structure from this additional variability. Although neural networks provided better overall fits to behavior than the traditional model, long-horizon choices remained consistently less predictable than short-horizon choices. These findings show that limited model expressiveness cannot fully account for the increased variability associated with random exploration, suggesting random exploration truly is substantially random.
item.dc:creator: Yingkang Luo, Hua-Dong Xiong, Hanbo Xie, Caroline Phelps, Madeline Harms, Ryan Smith, James Waltz, Robert Wilson

item.title: Parameter Symmetries Determine Representational Geometry in Overparameterized Nonlinear Networks
item.description: arXiv:2609.39078v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Representations are routinely used across machine learning, psychology, and neuroscience to draw inferences about the computations of biological and artificial systems. Such inferences presume that the geometry of these representations reflects the computation being performed. For artificial neural networks, however, the extent to which the function a network computes constrains this geometry remains unclear. One key obstacle is that these networks admit parameter symmetries: changes in parameterization that preserve function exactly while reshaping representational geometry. Here, we show that a broad class of parameter symmetries acts on representations through just three primitive feature transformations: addition, duplication, and scaling. This feature-level characterization yields a closed-form decomposition of representational geometry into essential and auxiliary components, revealing how representational degeneracy can exist without and grows with overparameterization even when function is held fixed. Finally, we establish conditions under which implementation-level selection rules resolve this degeneracy, yielding identifiable geometries in which features are weighted according to their contributions to the network's function. Together, our results delineate when representational geometry can support inferences about computation, and when it cannot.
item.dc:creator: Marvin Theiss, Lukas Braun, Andrew M. Saxe, Erin Grant

item.title: Alignment De-Identifies Without Aligning: A Congruence-Invariant Relational Gap in Cross-Subject Neural Representations
item.description: arXiv:2611.15204v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In brain-computer interfaces, inter-subject variability remains a major challenge that limits decoding performance across users. Subject-wise alignment is widely used to improve cross-subject transfer of neural decoders, yet it is typically evaluated only through decoding accuracy, which cannot determine whether aligned representations share greater task-related structure. We therefore distinguish two questions that accuracy conflates: whether alignment removes subject-specific information and whether it makes the relational organization of task conditions more similar across individuals. Using three motor imagery-EEG cohorts, trials are represented as covariance matrices and aligned by recentering each subject's mean covariance to a common reference. Subject-specific information is quantified with a subject-identification probe, whereas relational structure is assessed using representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs) computed from condition means with the affine-invariant Riemannian distance. We show that recentering leaves this distance, and therefore the resulting RDMs, unchanged. Consistent with this result, recentering reduces subject identification accuracy from 0.96 to chance level across all cohorts, while altering RDMs only at numerical precision. Cross-subject agreement in relational structure is significantly above zero but below the estimator's lower noise ceiling. Introducing an explicit similarity regularizer during training also fails to increase held-out agreement: the apparent reduction in between-subject differences is explained by a decline in the reliability ceiling rather than improved alignment. These findings show that eliminating subject identity is not equivalent to aligning relational geometry. More broadly, alignment claims must be interpreted relative to the invariances of both the distance and the statistic used to evaluate them.
item.dc:creator: Anna Notaro (University of Tuebingen, Germany), Letizia Rossato (Technical University of Denmark, Denmark), Sadasivan Puthusserypady (Technical University of Denmark, Denmark)

item.title: Exact power spectra and effective dimensionality in critical block-GOE networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.16427v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Criticality in neural networks is crucial for optimal information processing. Recent studies have shifted focus from static criticality to frequency-dependent behavior, particularly in oscillatory systems modeled by block-Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (block-GOE) matrices. However, analytical tools to predict spectral properties such as power spectrum and effective dimensionality remain scarce. In this work, we derive exact solutions for the network-averaged power spectrum $\operatorname{Tr}_{N}[\mathbf{S}(\omega)]$, the network autocovariance $\operatorname{Tr}_{N}[\mathbf{C}(\tau)]$, and the normalized effective dimensionality $D_N(\omega)$ in block-GOE ensembles. These results provide a comprehensive framework for understanding how oscillatory networks operate near criticality, offering insights into the dynamic balance between stability and flexibility in large-scale neural systems.
item.dc:creator: Konstantinos Grammenos, Dionissios Hristopulos

item.title: Similarity-Guided Optimization Strategies for Approximate Network Symmetry Detection
item.description: arXiv:2611.16555v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Symmetry in complex networks is a structural property with broad implications for network function, dynamics, and robustness. While classical approaches rely on exact automorphisms and thus remain highly sensitive to small perturbations, recent work of Liu has introduced approximate formulations that relax the strict invariance condition and recast symmetry detection as an optimization problem over permutations. We investigate how node-level similarity information can be used to bias the search toward structurally plausible vertex correspondences, with network centralities serving as one interpretable instance. Building on this perspective, we adapt simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, tabu search, particle swarm optimization, differential evolution and the quadratic symmetry approximator to this problem, add similarity guidance to each, and introduce Bilinear Approximate Symmetry Inference (BASIN), which learns a soft assignment matrix via bilinear embeddings. Using a unified evaluation pipeline, we compare their guided and unguided variants, BASIN and a random baseline on four synthetic graph families, structural brain connectomes, and three empirical networks with known automorphism groups. Node-similarity guidance is decisive where a planted orbit exists that the unguided search misses, and algorithm-dependent elsewhere, on synthetic and empirical networks alike. Overall, tabu search achieves the strongest performance; its guided variant (SGTS) has the lowest median score among the guided variants in all 44 synthetic conditions, while BASIN is the better of the continuous relaxations on rewired lateral graphs. The effect of node-similarity guidance is therefore regime-dependent rather than uniformly positive.
item.dc:creator: David Hartman, Jaroslav Hlinka, Dominik Klepl, Anna Pidnebesna, Petra Vidnerov\'a

item.title: On the minimum energy required to trigger a spike
item.description: arXiv:2611.16915v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We formulate and numerically study the problem of finding the minimum energy required to trigger a spike in a three-dimensional conductance-based excitable model. The variational formulation seeks a state trajectory that reaches the boundary of the spiking region with the least \textit{peak} cumulative work supplied through the membrane port. We approximate voltage histories by sums of real exponentials, reducing the problem to a finite-dimensional optimization. The best-found voltage waveform consists of a hyperpolarization phase followed by a depolarization phase, which seems to match the experimentally determined optimal stimulus in squid giant axons.
item.dc:creator: Guanchun Tong, Rodolphe Sepulchre

item.title: Structure-Preserving Leaky Integrate-and-Fire Dynamics on Arbitrary Time Scales
item.description: arXiv:2611.17219v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron combines a passive membrane law with threshold-triggered firing and reset. We formulate this hybrid neuron model, under constant input, on an arbitrary Hilger time scale $\mathbb{T}$. Our central result is that, after the first spike, the firing times satisfy $t_{n+1}=\Pi_{\mathbb{T}}^{+}(t_n+T_c)$, where $T_c$ is the classical reset-to-threshold travel time. This recursion requires no periodicity, homogeneity, or translation invariance of $\mathbb{T}$; it holds for every time scale that is unbounded above. To preserve the passive membrane physics, we use the inverse cylinder transformation to construct a positively regressive coefficient $p_m$. The resulting delta-dynamic equation is exactly the restriction to $\mathbb{T}$ of the classical continuous-time LIF trajectory. By contrast, the direct transcription $V^\Delta=-(V-V_\infty)/\tau_m$ exhibits graininess-dependent sign reversal and amplification at coarse right-scattered points. The first firing time is the forward projection of the classical continuous threshold-crossing time onto $\mathbb{T}$, and, when the graininess is bounded by $\mu^\ast$, the per-event forward-projection delay -- from each reset to the next realized firing time, relative to the continuous crossing time computed from that same reset -- is bounded above by $\mu^\ast$. On $\mathbb{T}=h\mathbb{Z}$ we obtain the explicit lattice-quantized law $T_{\mathrm{ISI}}^{(h)}=h\lceil T_c/h\rceil$, which converges to the classical continuous-time inter-spike interval as $h\to0^+$. The framework therefore separates preserved membrane physics from the temporal opportunity structure imposed by the time domain. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic Hilger-calculus treatment of a threshold-and-reset LIF spiking neuron on an arbitrary time scale.
item.dc:creator: Billur Kaymak\c{c}alan (University of Turkish Aeronautical Association), Behiye \.{I}layda Sel\c{c}uk (Bilkent University)

item.title: Lilith: Developmental Modular LLMs with Chemical Signaling
item.description: arXiv:2507.04575v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Current paradigms in Artificial Intelligence rely on layers of feedforward networks which model brain activity at the neuronal level. We conjecture that expanding to the level of multiple brain regions with chemical signaling may be a productive step toward understanding the emergence of consciousness. We propose LILITH, a novel architecture that combines developmental training of modular language models with brain-inspired token-based communication protocols, mirroring chemical signaling in the brain. Our approach models distinct brain regions as specialized LLM modules including thinking, memory, sensory, and regulatory components that communicate through emergent token-based signaling protocols analogous to neurotransmitter networks. Unlike traditional pre-trained systems, LILITH would employ developmental training where untrained LLM architectures learn through simulated life experiences, developing communication pathways and cognitive abilities through environmental interaction and evolutionary optimization. This framework would enable direct empirical investigation of consciousness emergence using Integrated Information Theory metrics while providing unprecedented insight into inter-module signaling patterns during development. By optimizing for consciousness emergence rather than task performance, LILITH could provide insight into different emergent phenomena at multiple levels of neural correlates, contrasting neuronal-level processing with multi-region coordination dynamics. The goal of this paper is to put the idea forward while recognizing the substantial challenges in implementing such a system.
item.dc:creator: Mohid Farooqi, Alejandro Comas-Leon

item.title: Reduced rank regression for neural communication: a tutorial for neuroscientists
item.description: arXiv:2512.12467v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reduced rank regression (RRR) is a statistical method for finding a low-dimensional linear mapping between a set of high-dimensional inputs and outputs. In recent years, RRR has found numerous applications in neuroscience, in particular for identifying "communication subspaces" governing the interactions between brain regions. This tutorial article seeks to provide an introduction to RRR and its mathematical foundations, with a particular emphasis on neural communication. We discuss RRR's relationship to alternate dimensionality reduction techniques such as singular value decomposition (SVD), principal components analysis (PCA), principal components regression (PCR), and canonical correlation analysis (CCA). We also derive important extensions to RRR, including ridge regularization and non-spherical noise. Finally, we introduce new metrics for quantifying communication strength as well as the alignment between communication axes and the principal modes of neural activity. By the end of this article, readers should have a clear understanding of RRR and the practical considerations involved in applying it to their own data.
item.dc:creator: Bichan Wu, Jonathan Pillow

item.title: Recognizing Mind Wandering: A Computational Phenomenology of Focused-Attention Meditation
item.description: arXiv:2607.14833v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mind wandering often continues without recognition, raising a question about the relationship between attention and consciousness. How can a distraction be experienced before it is recognized as an attentional lapse, and what does recognition change? We address it for mind wandering, a form of spontaneous thought, during focused-attention meditation on the breath, through a computational phenomenology informed by Buddhist analyses of mind and meditation neuroscience. In an active-inference-inspired three-layer architecture, mental contents, termed thoughtseeds, are inferred from simulated large-scale brain network activity and compete for a capacity-limited global workspace, whose selection parallels Bengio's consciousness prior, while a separate graded monitor supports discrete recognition of lapses. Within a specified cycle of Breath Focus, Mind Wandering, Meta Awareness and Redirect Attention, recognition could begin while a distraction still held the workspace, an overlap that was usually brief. Stochastic monitoring checks also allowed intermittent recognition during ongoing wandering, with long intervals unrecognized. Recognition releases stabilization of the current regime and modulates the return policy in Meta Awareness, while return remains possible without it. Breath re-entry, recognition and redirection need not coincide. The model thus separates access to distracting content, monitoring of attention and recognition of a lapse, and shows how awareness of wandering can change its regulation without immediately ending it. This framework could be adapted to other meditation practices, to practice-related differences between novice and expert meditators, and to modeling subjective experience in other cognitive tasks.
item.dc:creator: Prakash Chandra Kavi, Daniel Ari Friedman, Gustavo Patow

item.title: The Platonic brain bridge hypothesis: brain networks as architectural priors for multimodal large language models
item.description: arXiv:2609.10947v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multimodal large language models predict brain activity, but alignment has remained a measurement, not a design tool. We propose the Platonic brain bridge hypothesis: omni models, which jointly process video, audio and text, share brain-like representations usable in both directions. From model to brain, seven omni models show stable brain-likeness across participants, and our encoding experts lead the Algonauts 2025 out-of-distribution leaderboard by mean score. From brain to model, we make three contributions. Brain-MoE ties the experts of a frozen model to the seven cortical networks, raises held-out accuracy in all 15 model-benchmark pairs and exceeds capacity-matched random experts in 14. Brain-AVQA, to our knowledge the first audiovisual benchmark with cortical-network labels for every question, supplies the pretraining questions. Brain-Scope finds sparse features that predict brain responses, steer routing and, when removed, weaken brain prediction. Human brain organization is therefore a usable architectural prior for multimodal large language models.
item.dc:creator: Pengfei Zhang, Biao Tian, Xiangang Li, Li Liu

item.title: Planning as Dynamics Relaxation: Hippocampal Recurrent Network Realizes Optimal Goal-Directed Navigation
item.description: arXiv:2609.13219v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neural correlates of the cognitive map are well documented, yet how a neural circuit turns a stored map into an obstacle-avoiding route remains unclear. Here we show that a hippocampal network with appropriate recurrent connections achieves optimal goal-directed navigation through its own relaxation dynamics. The recurrent weights represent the transition probabilities between the locations the neurons encode, walls are reflected by vanishing weights, and behavioral-timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP) writes this connectivity during goal-free exploration. When a goal is recalled, a top-down current clamps the goal neuron and the population relaxes into a goal-locked activity field. We prove that this field is the desirability field of a linearly-solvable Markov decision process: the relaxed state is the exact optimum of a stated control problem, the KL-regularized objective of Todorov, and the optimal next-step distribution is carried by the branch synaptic currents. The identity extends to directed transitions, and a weak-cost limit returns the Green's function of the recurrent Laplacian. A place-tuned readout converts the field's log-gradient into a direction of travel, and the same synapses answer a predictive query when the source is placed at the current location. Simulations on mazes with complex obstacles show near-shortest routes, an identity that survives a thousand-fold range of recall amplitude, the loss of 80% of place cells, and tens of thousands of states, low-rank updates of every plan after a local change, and a transient that is anytime: the local action is ready long before the field converges. We hope this offers a general circuit principle for planning in abstract cognitive maps beyond spatial navigation.
item.dc:creator: Yuhang He, Junfeng Zuo, Tianhao Chu, Si Wu

item.title: A theory of plasticity: capacity for change as inverse configurational constraint
item.description: arXiv:2609.25312v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Plasticity is invoked across the sciences to explain how systems can change, yet it is inferred from the very change it is meant to explain. A system may have many alternatives, realize none and still be plastic. Another may be driven far toward its only alternative, but the magnitude of that change does not establish its plasticity. What matters for plasticity is not how far the system moves but how strongly its present configuration constrains alternatives. Here I propose that plasticity, understood as a prospective property, is inverse configurational constraint: a system is plastic to the extent that its present configuration weakly constrains displacement toward alternatives within a declared representation. For systems sharing a functional partition, structural representation, and normalized architecture, increasing plasticity lowers every positive finite structural barrier separating the current state from its alternatives. With a fixed accessibility criterion, the accessible repertoire can expand but cannot shrink. In network representations, aggregate coupling is identified as configurational constraint, whose inverse defines plasticity. Barrier reduction and repertoire nesting are consequences, not components, of the definition. This connects two research traditions: quantifying connectivity without interpreting it as plasticity, and treating plasticity as a capacity for change without a prospective operational measure.
item.dc:creator: Igor Branchi

item.title: Fine-Tuning Language Models to Know What They Know
item.description: arXiv:2602.02605v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Evaluating true metacognition in Large Language Models (LLMs) is difficult due to biases and heuristics. This paper presents a framework to measure and enhance LLM metacognition while controlling for these biases. A measurement method using the $d'_{\rm type2}$ metric is established to isolate metacognitive ability. The Evolution Strategy for Metacognitive Alignment (ESMA) is proposed, demonstrating robust generalization across unseen datasets, languages, and newly acquired knowledge. Gradual parameter updates reveal that these improvements are driven by a sparse set of parameters, opening a potential avenue for targeted metacognitive optimization.
item.dc:creator: Sangjun Park, Elliot Meyerson, Xin Qiu, Risto Miikkulainen

item.title: Measuring Robustness and Efficiency in a Connectome-Constrained Fly Visual System Model: Linking an Adversarial and a Perceptual Illusion
item.description: arXiv:2611.14498v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Biological visual systems compute reliably under tight metabolic and wiring constraints, whereas artificial vision systems consume far more energy and can be sensitive to adversarial perturbations. Whether networks with brain-like wiring are more robust at lower computational cost is unclear. We address this by benchmarking a task-optimized, continuous-time recurrent neural network of the fly visual system constrained by its synaptic connectome (FlyNet) against artificial neural networks. We compare it against CNNs, RAFT, and continuous-time recurrent neural networks without detailed connectome constraints (sCTRNN, CTRNN) on a collision-detection task within a differentiable 3D rendering pipeline. FlyNet is adversarially vulnerable but, relative to its compute, more robust to common video corruptions than RAFT, while using up to five orders of magnitude fewer FLOPs. The CTRNNs remain more robust than FlyNet across almost all tested perturbations, suggesting that connectome constraints benefit efficiency, through their low edge count, over robustness. Recurrence improves robustness to white-box attacks in RAFT and temporal context improves robustness to common corruptions. FlyNet's position and velocity representations degrade under adversarial textures but recover under counterfactual textures that restore correct classification while staying equally far from training, ruling out unfamiliar textures as the cause of failure. The reverse-phi illusion similarly disrupts these representations and inverts the same low-level motion statistic as the adversarial textures. Optimizing this input statistic alone, without access to the network, suffices to induce classification failure, attributing both perturbations to the same circuit vulnerability. Connectome-constrained models can thus surface adversarial failure mechanisms as testable hypotheses about biological perceptual vulnerabilities.
item.dc:creator: Alexandre Garcia-Duran, Alejandro Rodriguez-Garcia, Manuel Molano-Maz\'on, Alexandre Hyafil, Srikanth Ramaswamy, Janne K. Lappalainen
